doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Ruby Braff: trio, bandstand brilliance and his health
summary: Tate praises Braff's trio, his fearlessness, and discusses his health.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: What’s it like working with Ruby? © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

The best. Yeah. I miss him. Because I was in his trio for three, a couple, two, three years. We rehearsed the first time up at my house in Croton-on-Hudson. And Howard brought Ruby up. And Ruby and I had never played together. And we were in my old study. And Howard’s [scats] swinging like mad. Ruby’s playing and Ruby’s making, he’s going [scats] and I knew immediately that he was digging it. And that trio was so good. We were so together there for a while. We made some nice records and did some good gigs and concerts. It was really, really sensational. And Ruby’s at his best on the bandstand. That’s the time that he enjoys the most. Everything else is marking time with him, waiting to get on the bandstand, as best I can figure him out. I mean I think it’s what he really lives for. And he’s passionately involved with it while it’s happening. And he has a knack of leading — he led a group with seven or eight musicians last night and made it sound like they’d been on the road. He’s directing traffic, pointing to this guy and that guy and working out things while it’s — and a really devil may care attitude about — he’ll go for anything. And when he goes for it he gets it, and he goes way down on the bottom of the horn like nobody can. His lower register is — and that’s tough sledding down there. The fingerings are all awkward, those are the hardest fingerings, the bottom part of the horn are the ones where you’ve got to use two and three, one two and three, one and three, and it’s very heavy and cumbersome, the fingering. And he’s just down there wailing in the lower register. He’s fearless.
Great to hear that about him.

He’s 74 and I shouldn’t comment about his health except to say I don’t think he’s doing so well. And everybody says, “Well if he’s got a breathing problem, how can he play the trumpet?” Well if you look at the trumpet, the bell is this big around but there’s not a column of air coming out. The column of air is this big around going into the mouthpiece. So that isn’t the problem. It’s just feeling well enough to go out there and put joy into it. And how he does it I don’t know, he just gets up there, like last night it was earth shatteringly good music last night. And it was all because of him at the helm. I miss not working with him. Well I’m looking forward to this gig coming up this coming Tuesday because he’ll have had a couple of days down here playing and we’re traveling the day before so we’ll be well rested, and we got Bill Charlap. Yeah. Wow. Where did this guy come from? Well I know where he came from, his father was Ray Charlap the writer and his mother is Sandy Stewart. I was talking about her the other night and I said Sandy Dennis or Sandy Duncan or something. And Bobby was laughing and he said, “No, you moron.” I know who she is she’s a club singer. A good singer. Broadway and cabaret I think. So he’s on it and that’ll be fun, a nice gig.
